documents.title: Academic Integrity Policy
documents.summary: Tier 1: Short school-level academic integrity statement for computer science. It frames programming assignments as learning opportunities, defines submitting code one did not write (including AI-generated code from tools such as Copilot or ChatGPT) as plagiarism, and makes this the school default unless a syllabus or assignment allows generated code.

excerpts.text: Students who submit code that they did not write are both missing a learning opportunity
This includes copying code found on websites or having AI generate the code for you

the Jodrey School of Computer Science will treat AI-generated work as plagiarism
unless the syllabus/assignment direction specifically allows for the use of such generated code

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence at Cape Breton University: AI With a Purpose
documents.summary: Tier 4: Institution-wide, principle-based AI strategy (People First, Prudence, Accountability) rather than a rulebook. It declines universal rules, ties AI in teaching to existing academic integrity standards and the priority on critical thinking, and flags privacy, bias, copyright and environmental concerns; it is a living document overseen by an accountability committee.

documents.title: Algoma University: Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Generative AI by Students
documents.date_or_term: Approved by Algoma University Senate May 2, 2025
documents.summary: Tier 4: Senate-approved student guidelines that prohibit generative AI in all coursework unless the instructor explicitly permits it, and require written permission before use. Where AI is allowed, students must cite it, verify outputs and protect their privacy; instructors may use AI detectors, and sanctions range from a zero on the assignment or course to suspension or expulsion.

documents.title: Generative AI Guide for Instructors
documents.summary: Tier 4: Senate-approved instructor guide. The university does not restrict AI, so each instructor decides and must state the course rule and the expected citation format on the syllabus. It advises against banning specific tools and against AI detectors, forbids submitting student work to AI tools, notes AI's code-generation abilities, and suggests assessment redesign and equity limits on paid tools. A mandatory academic integrity course covers GenAI rules.
